newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada sends Saudi bombing suspect to U.S..
newsitem.headline: Canada sends Saudi bombing suspect to U.S..

text.p: Canada on Tuesday deported to the United States a Saudi man suspected of being involved in the truck bomb that killed 19 U.S. airmen in Saudi Arabia, Citizenship and Immigration spokesman Rene Mercier said.

The suspect, Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh, was taken from an Ottawa prison and flown to the United States under an arrangement that appeared to assure him he would not be charged in the attack last June.

Canadian authorities ruled last month he should be deported as a suspected terrorist but it was not clear then whether he would go to the United States or Saudi Arabia, where his wife and two daughters still live.

Sayegh opposed deportation to Saudi Arabia, where his New York lawyer, Michael Wildes, said he would have faced execution. Wildes said the deal with the United States protected both his safety and U.S. government interests.
FBI authorities have sought to interrogate him to try to find out who was behind the blast, which injured hundreds of others.

"After negotiations between departmental officials and Mr. al-Sayegh about his removal from Canada, Mr. al-Sayegh elected to be removed to the United States," a statement from Canadian Citizenship and Immigration Department said.
The statement said he left Ottawa escorted by Royal Canadian Mounted Police and Immigration officials.

Sayegh, 29, a Shi'ite Muslim, had been identified in Canadian court documents as the driver of a car that gave the go-ahead signal for the bomb-laden truck in the attack on Khobar Towers in Dhahran, eastern Saudi Arabia.

The documents also said he was a member of the radical Saudi Hizbollah (Party of God). Sayegh has claimed he had no involvement in the attack, though sources close to him said he may know others who had been named.
"He clearly is a minority Shi'ite and has been outspoken on his pro-democracy beliefs," Wildes told Reuters from New York.
"If only for those political beliefs he would be executed. Because of the sensitive nature of the intelligence that he has, he would most certainly meet with death if he returns to Saudi Arabia."
Details of the deal with the United States were sealed until Sayegh's scheduled appearance with Wildes in federal court Wednesday in Washington.
U.S. officials in Washington said he would tell U.S. authorities what he knew about the bombing and would plead guilty to conspiracy charges involving an unrelated attack plotted in the Middle East.
A source in Canada said Sayegh, quiet and clean-cut, would take a lie-detector test concerning his claim he was not involved in the Khobar Towers attack.
